Lessons.Title: The Root of the Problem
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Recover a positive linear scale from a prescribed volume factor with the cube-root function; contrast it with the square root needed for surface area.
Mathematical model: If volume ratio q=k³ with k>0, length factor is k=∛q Use the real positive cube root A known volume ratio q implies area ratio q^(2/3)
Application and limitations: Nonnegative geometric volumes yield nonnegative scale factors Positive nondegenerate solids require q>0

Authentic source-specific activity: Plot k↦k³ and positive cube root; explain graph axes as scale and volume ratio. Teacher reviews interpretation and inverse-function argument. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct diagram/units, explicit premises, reliable calculations, and an independently justified interpretation. Original drawings and written reasoning require teacher scoring.
Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 7, CC BY 4.0. Independent first-party Edulytiks examples; no publisher artwork or protected assessments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cube-root inverse
KeyConcepts.Definition: If volume ratio q=k³ with k>0, length factor is k=∛q
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use the real positive cube root

KeyConcepts.Title: Surface-area comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Surface area ratio is k², distinct from k³
KeyConcepts.Rule: A known volume ratio q implies area ratio q^(2/3)

KeyConcepts.Title: Model domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: Nonnegative geometric volumes yield nonnegative scale factors

WorkedExamples.Title: The Root of the Problem — example 3
WorkedExamples.Question: A cube has volume 343 cm³. What is its edge length?
WorkedExamples.Check: Check each hypothesis, unit and numerical result against positive nondegenerate solids require q>0

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Taking square root of volume factor
Treating negative volume factor as physical
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A real positive volume cannot become negative under positive dilation

SummaryPoints: Recover a positive linear scale from a prescribed volume factor with the cube-root function; contrast it with the square root needed for surface area.
A known volume ratio q implies area ratio q^(2/3)

Lessons.Title: Speaking of Scaling
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Coordinate length, surface-area and volume scale factors in both forward and reverse directions from any one known ratio, and communicate missing information.
Mathematical model: For uniform dilation, ratios are k,k²,k³ Use positive roots for inverse problems Reversed area and volume factors are 1/k² and 1/k³
Application and limitations: The type of given ratio must be specified to find the others Ask whether a value is a length, area or volume ratio

Authentic source-specific activity: Pairs exchange partial length/area/volume factor cards and justify complete factors without viewing each other's original data. Teacher scores questions and reasoning. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct diagram/units, explicit premises, reliable calculations, and an independently justified interpretation. Original drawings and written reasoning require teacher scoring.
Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 8, CC BY 4.0. Independent first-party Edulytiks examples; no publisher artwork or protected assessments.

KeyConcepts.Title: One factor determines others
KeyConcepts.Definition: For uniform dilation, ratios are k,k²,k³
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use positive roots for inverse problems
KeyConcepts.Example: Area factor 36 gives k=6 and volume factor 216

KeyConcepts.Title: Reverse scaling
KeyConcepts.Definition: Inverting a dilation replaces k by 1/k
KeyConcepts.Rule: Reversed area and volume factors are 1/k² and 1/k³

KeyConcepts.Title: Information-gaps
KeyConcepts.Definition: The type of given ratio must be specified to find the others
KeyConcepts.Rule: Ask whether a value is a length, area or volume ratio
KeyConcepts.Example: Given only 'ratio 8' without dimension type is ambiguous

WorkedExamples.Title: Speaking of Scaling — example 1
WorkedExamples.Question: A scale model has surface area 25 times its prototype. Find length and volume factors.
WorkedExamples.Check: Check each hypothesis, unit and numerical result against use positive roots for inverse problems

WorkedExamples.Title: Speaking of Scaling — example 2
WorkedExamples.Question: A 3D design is scaled up 2× and then scaled back; give the second volume factor.
WorkedExamples.Check: Check each hypothesis, unit and numerical result against reversed area and volume factors are 1/k² and 1/k³

WorkedExamples.Title: Speaking of Scaling — example 3
WorkedExamples.Question: An engineer reports new volume is 1/27 of original. Find surface ratio.
WorkedExamples.Check: Check each hypothesis, unit and numerical result against ask whether a value is a length, area or volume ratio

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a reported volume factor as a length factor
Inverting k but not the corresponding powered factor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Reverse scale requires reciprocal of each dimensional factor

SummaryPoints: Coordinate length, surface-area and volume scale factors in both forward and reverse directions from any one known ratio, and communicate missing information.
Reversed area and volume factors are 1/k² and 1/k³
Teacher-reviewed diagrams and reasoning remain necessary for academic acceptance.

Lessons.Title: Cylinder Volumes
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Derive and use V=πr²h for right or oblique circular cylinders, and compute volumes of composite figures and rotational solids without confusing radius with diameter.
Mathematical model: A cylinder has constant cross-sectional disk area B=πr² Volume=Bh=πr²h with perpendicular height h Cavalieri gives same volume for equal base area and perpendicular height
Application and limitations: Volumes add for disjoint interiors and subtract removed pieces Use consistent cubic units

Authentic source-specific activity: Model a rolled rectangle as a cylinder and compare prism stacks and cylinder cross sections; teacher evaluates geometry and justified formula. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct diagram/units, explicit premises, reliable calculations, and an independently justified interpretation. Original drawings and written reasoning require teacher scoring.
Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 9, CC BY 4.0. Independent first-party Edulytiks examples; no publisher artwork or protected assessments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Composite solid
KeyConcepts.Definition: Volumes add for disjoint interiors and subtract removed pieces
KeyConcepts.Example: Cylinder with axial hole has π(R²−r²)h

Lessons.Title: Cross Sections and Volume
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Apply Cavalieri's principle correctly: solids of equal height with equal cross-sectional areas at each corresponding level have equal volumes; compare oblique prisms and cylinders.
Mathematical model: Equal-height solids with matching areas of parallel sections at every corresponding height have equal volumes Require all levels, not one Constant A gives V=Ah
Application and limitations: Equal base area or one equal slice alone does not force equal volume Check all corresponding levels

Authentic source-specific activity: Build original stack diagrams and explain why shearing constant-area slices preserves volume; teacher reviews all-level reasoning. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct diagram/units, explicit premises, reliable calculations, and an independently justified interpretation. Original drawings and written reasoning require teacher scoring.

Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 10, CC BY 4.0. Independent first-party Edulytiks examples; no publisher artwork or protected assessments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cavalieri's principle
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal-height solids with matching areas of parallel sections at every corresponding height have equal volumes
KeyConcepts.Example: An oblique prism and right prism of same base area and height have equal volumes

KeyConcepts.Title: Slice integral intuition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Volume accumulates parallel cross-sectional areas through height

KeyConcepts.Title: Counterexample
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal base area or one equal slice alone does not force equal volume
KeyConcepts.Example: Cone and cylinder of equal base/height have different volume

WorkedExamples.Title: Cross Sections and Volume — example 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Right and oblique prisms each have base area 12 cm² and perpendicular height 7 cm. Compare volumes.
Steps: Every horizontal cross-section of each prism has area 12
WorkedExamples.Check: Check each hypothesis, unit and numerical result against require all levels, not one

WorkedExamples.Title: Cross Sections and Volume — example 2
WorkedExamples.Question: A stack of disks has constant disk area 9π cm² for height 5. Find volume.
WorkedExamples.Check: Check each hypothesis, unit and numerical result against constant a gives v=ah

WorkedExamples.Title: Cross Sections and Volume — example 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Can matching base area 20 and height 6 guarantee a cone and cylinder equal volumes?
Steps: Sections differ at interior levels so Cavalieri conditions fail
WorkedExamples.Answer: No: cylinder 120 and cone 40 cubic units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Check each hypothesis, unit and numerical result against check all corresponding levels

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The matching heights must be perpendicular to slicing planes

SummaryPoints: Apply Cavalieri's principle correctly: solids of equal height with equal cross-sectional areas at each corresponding level have equal volumes; compare oblique prisms and cylinders.
Teacher-reviewed diagrams and reasoning remain necessary for academic acceptance.

ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Solve composite volumes involving right and oblique prisms, converting between base area, perimeter and perpendicular height, and distinguishing a slanted side from height.
Mathematical model: Every prism has congruent parallel cross sections V=Bh Use perpendicular base separation
Application and limitations: Add nonoverlapping pieces or subtract voids Track cm²×cm=cm³

Lessons.Title: Prisms and Pyramids
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Contrast prisms, pyramids, cylinders and cones by their changing versus constant parallel cross sections and predict the one-third volume relationship.
Mathematical model: Prism parallel slices are congruent; pyramid slices shrink toward one apex Identify base, apex and perpendicular height Equal base and height do not imply equal volume
Application and limitations: A pyramid and prism with same base area B and height h have ratio 1:3 Use established decomposition/Cavalieri formula

Authentic source-specific activity: Draw labelled constant-section and taper-section sequences and justify why cone/pyramid differ from prism/cylinder. Teacher reviews arguments. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct diagram/units, explicit premises, reliable calculations, and an independently justified interpretation. Original drawings and written reasoning require teacher scoring.

Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 12, CC BY 4.0. Independent first-party Edulytiks examples; no publisher artwork or protected assessments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Prism vs pyramid
KeyConcepts.Definition: Prism parallel slices are congruent; pyramid slices shrink toward one apex
KeyConcepts.Rule: Identify base, apex and perpendicular height

KeyConcepts.Title: Cone vs cylinder
KeyConcepts.Definition: Cone parallel disks taper; cylinder disks have constant area
KeyConcepts.Rule: Equal base and height do not imply equal volume
KeyConcepts.Example: Cone volume is one third matching cylinder

KeyConcepts.Title: Volume comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: A pyramid and prism with same base area B and height h have ratio 1:3
